title: Completion and the etale criterion for finite rank-one valued extensions
statement: Let $F\subseteq E$ be a finite extension of fields with compatible nontrivial nonarchimedean real absolute values [def-weil-field], with valuation rings $A=\{a\in F:|a|\leq1\}$ and $B=\{b\in E:|b|\leq1\}$ [def-trf-valuation-ring], and let $\widehat F\subseteq\widehat E$ be their metric completions. Then $\widehat E/\widehat F$ is finite, of degree at most $[E:F]$, and completion induces isomorphisms on residue fields (the quotients of the valuation rings by their elements of absolute value less than one). The map $A\to B$ is etale [def-weil-etale-morphism] if and only if $E/F$ is separable [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension] and the valuation ring of $\widehat E$ is etale over that of $\widehat F$.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.1 and its proof, printed p. 11; preliminary facts on completions used there; Lemma 2.1.6 for the etale terminology.

proof.text: The isometric inclusion extends to $\widehat F\hookrightarrow\widehat E$, giving continuous scalar multiplication. Choose an $F$-basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ of $E$, where $n=[E:F]$. Its $\widehat F$-span $U\subseteq\widehat E$ has dimension at most $n$. It is closed by [lem-sfb-finite-dimensional-subspace-closed], over the nontrivially normed complete field $\widehat F$. It contains the dense subfield $E$, so $U=\widehat E$. This proves finiteness and the degree bound without separability.

source.place: Preliminary completion fact used in Proposition 2.2.1; span-and-density details supplied by Q81.

proof.text: For $H=F$ or $E$, completion preserves absolute values, so its kernel on residue classes is exactly $\{h:|h|<1\}$. If $u\in\widehat H$ satisfies $|u|\leq1$, choose $h\in H$ with $|u-h|<1$. Then $|h|\leq1$ and $h,u$ have the same residue. Thus both residue maps are isomorphisms, compatibly with the field inclusion. Choose $a\in F$ with $0<|a|<1$. Since $|a|^N\to0$, every element in any of the four fields becomes integral after multiplication by a power of $a$. Hence $A[1/a]=F$, $B[1/a]=E$, $\widehat A[1/a]=\widehat F$ and $\widehat B[1/a]=\widehat E$, where $\widehat A,\widehat B$ denote the completed valuation rings.

source.place: Elementary density, residue and rank-one generic-fibre identifications.

proof.text: Suppose $A\to B$ is etale. Base change to $F=A[1/a]$ is etale by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-scheme-base-change], with ring $B[1/a]=E$ by step 2. The etale-field-algebra theorem [lem-weil-pbc-etale-algebra-over-field-product] makes $E$ a product of finite separable $F$-fields. A nonzero field has no nontrivial product decomposition, so $E/F$ is separable.

Set $D=B\otimes_A\widehat A$, etale over $\widehat A$ by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-scheme-base-change]. Let $\mathfrak n$ be the inverse image of the maximal ideal under $D\to\widehat B$, $b\otimes c\mapsto bc$. It lies over the maximal ideal of $\widehat A$. Since $E/F$ is separable by step 3, [lem-trf-separable-valued-completion-factors] applies: $\widehat A$ is henselian and $D[1/a]=E\otimes_F\widehat F$ is the product of the completed branches. By [lem-trf-henselian-valuation-etale-local-factors], $D_{\mathfrak n}$ is finite etale and the unique valuation ring of its fraction field extending $\widehat A$. The map $D_{\mathfrak n}\to\widehat B$ selects the given generic factor: after inverting $a$, localization of the product of fields at its selected prime is exactly $\widehat E$. Thus its fraction field is $\widehat E$, and uniqueness identifies $D_{\mathfrak n}=\widehat B$. Hence $\widehat A\to\widehat B$ is etale.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.1, forward implication, local factor of the base-changed etale algebra.

proof.text: Conversely suppose $E/F$ is separable and $\widehat A\to\widehat B$ is etale. Let $C$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $E$. By [lem-trf-separable-valued-completion-factors] it has finitely many maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_i$, indexed so $B=C_{\mathfrak m_1}$, and completed branches $\widehat E_i$ with $\widehat E_1=\widehat E$. Apply [lem-trf-henselian-valuation-etale-local-factors] to $R=\widehat A$, $D=\widehat B$ and its maximal ideal. Since $\widehat B$ is already local, it is finite etale, its residue field is finite separable, and the residue-generator conclusions apply. Step 2 identifies the residue extension with $A/\mathfrak m_A\subseteq C/\mathfrak m_1$.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.1, converse: semilocal normalization and the finite etale completed branch.

proof.text: By [lem-trf-primitive-element-separated-valuations] choose $x\in C$ primitive for $E/F$, with nonzero primitive residue in $C/\mathfrak m_1$ and $x\in\mathfrak m_i$ for $i>1$. By [lem-trf-separable-valued-completion-factors] its monic minimal polynomial belongs to $A[T]$ and factors $f=\prod_i f_i$ in $\widehat A[T]$, with $f_i$ the minimal polynomial of its image $x_i\in\widehat E_i$, and all roots of $f_i$ of absolute value $|x|_i$. By [lem-trf-henselian-valuation-etale-local-factors] on the chosen branch, $\overline f_1$ is the separable minimal polynomial of $\bar x$, so $f_1'(x_1)$ is a unit of $\widehat B$.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.1, converse: separated primitive element and the chosen irreducible factor.

proof.text:
For $i>1$, every root of $f_i$ has absolute value $|x|_i<1$. Every nonleading coefficient is an elementary symmetric sum of products of positive numbers of roots, so has absolute value less than one. Thus $\overline f_i=T^{d_i}$ for $d_i=\deg f_i$. Since $\bar x\ne0$, the residue of $f_i(x_1)$ is $\bar x^{d_i}\ne0$, so it is a unit. Differentiating the product and using $f_1(x_1)=0$ gives
$$f'(x_1)=f_1'(x_1)\prod_{i>1}f_i(x_1),$$
a unit by step 6. The isometric inclusion $B\hookrightarrow\widehat B$ reflects absolute value one, hence $f'(x)$ is a unit in $B$. For one branch the empty product equals $1$.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.1, converse, explicit elementary polynomial-factor computation.

proof.text: The subring $D=A[x,1/f'(x)]\subseteq B$ is isomorphic to $A[T]_{f'}/(f)$: division by the monic $f$ shows that a polynomial over $A$ vanishing at $x$ is divisible by $f$ already over $A$. By [lem-weil-pbc-standard-etale-monic-derivative], $D$ is etale over $A$. Its fraction field is $E$ since $x$ is primitive. By [lem-weil-pbc-valuation-ring-normal] and [lem-weil-pbc-etale-over-normal-ring-normal], $D$ is a normal domain. Every element of $C$ is integral over $A\subseteq D$, hence over $D$, and thus belongs to $D$. Put $\mathfrak n=D\cap\mathfrak m_B$. From $C\subseteq D\subseteq B$ we obtain $C_{\mathfrak m_1}\subseteq D_{\mathfrak n}\subseteq B$ by inverting elements with nonzero residue. Since $C_{\mathfrak m_1}=B$, we get $D_{\mathfrak n}=B$.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.1, converse: normal standard etale subring and its selected localization.

proof.text: We make the localization etale rather than merely essentially etale. The only primes of $A$ are $(0)$ and $\mathfrak m_A$: if a nonzero prime contains $b\ne0$ with $|b|<1$, then for every $c$ with $|c|<1$ some $N$ has $c^N/b\in A$, so $c^N\in(b)$ and $c$ is in the prime. The generic fibre $D[1/a]=E$ has one prime, $(0)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-etale-scheme-base-change] and [lem-weil-pbc-etale-algebra-over-field-product], the closed fibre is a finite product of fields. Thus the other primes of $D$ are finitely many distinct maximal ideals $\mathfrak n=\mathfrak n_1,\ldots,\mathfrak n_s$. Choose $t_j\in\mathfrak n_j\setminus\mathfrak n$ for $j>1$ and set $t=\prod_{j>1}t_j$, or $t=1$ if $s=1$. The ring $D_t$ has just one maximal ideal $\mathfrak nD_t$, so every element of $D\setminus\mathfrak n$ is invertible there. Consequently $D_t=D_{\mathfrak n}=B$. By [lem-weil-pbc-etale-algebra-finite-presentation-localization], this localization at one element is etale over $A$, as required.

source.place: Lemma 2.1.1 and Proposition 2.2.1, last sentence; explicit rank-one finite-spectrum argument.
